item.title: Coping After Brain Injury
item.description:
Traumatic Brain Injury

Coping After Brain Injury

What does research say about coping styles after an acquired brain injury?

Posted August 18, 2026

Source: Pedro Figueras/Pixabay

In 2001, during my outpatient neurorehab at the Toronto Rehabilitation Institute (TRI), I enrolled in a 10-week stress management course as part of TRI’s clinical research. TRI tested our stress levels and had us rate our primary coping strategies. At that point, I was still grappling with my closed head injury diagnosis, understood I had a brain injury, and falsely believed that I’d be better soon, for I had not grasped that the medical system didn’t provide healing treatments and their strategies wouldn’t restore neurons and neural networks. As a result, I understood the test results but not the ramifications on my life or my familiar coping methods.

My top coping strategy prior to my brain injury was reading, and years later, brain biofeedback proved its physiological relaxation effect.

Prior to my brain injury, I read every day. I read newspapers in the morning; novels over lunch and during afternoon breaks; materials for my work throughout the day; literary tomes as a challenging habit; and emails and e-newsletters. I visited the library weekly and restricted myself to three mystery mass paperbacks per week. I could’ve read five. That was my biggest regret after brain injury: listening to complaints about my prodigious reading and cutting back, even though I read when they weren’t around or while keeping them company during TV watching.

About three months before I enrolled in the stress management course, my rehab team had informed me I couldn’t read anymore. The stress management assessment showed me reading as my top coping strategy; eating ice cream and chocolate as second. Guess which one became the top one by default?

Worse, my Life Change Index showed an 80 percent likelihood of experiencing illness in the near future. I had the worst combination: the highest stress levels, the loss of my top coping mechanism, and the elevation of an unhealthy coping strategy, which, along with changes to my hunger and appetite signals, created a new habit of eating when not hungry. My hair fell out.

Eighteen years later, I regained my top strategy, but I continue to struggle with incorporating reading in my stress management and with not using eating as stress management.

In 2001, TRI taught us post-injury coping strategies, but brain injury makes a mockery of retention, which the course and subsequent healthcare didn’t consider. As a result, coping for me became a stop-start series of learning, forgetting, experimenting, and some functional methods that reflected my drive to get better.

Research by Lazarus in 1993 contrasted two theories of coping: a personality trait versus an adaptive skill. Sasse et al in 2014 discussed two types of strategies: adaptive action/distraction versus maladaptive trivialization/resignation. A 2000 study by Bryant et al concluded “that reduction of PTSD and management of severe TBI may be facilitated by teaching patients more adaptive coping strategies.” They identified avoidant as maladaptive.

A 2024 overview study noted, “Coping strategies are essential for clinical recovery and for dealing with the stressful events that a clinical condition brings with it.” Of the 2,593 studies selected for review, Cardile et al analyzed 16 that met their inclusion criteria. “Research has shown that patients with ABI who use active coping strategies and are problem-oriented face the disease with greater resilience and a sense of self-efficacy and report fewer symptoms.”

article continues after advertisement

Although I take issue with characterizing an injury as a disease, this conclusion dovetails with my experience as a person who identifies a problem, works to understand it, and seeks to resolve it. So is coping a combination of personality and acquired skills?

In 2014, Australian researchers studied pre-injury versus post-injury coping changes. They categorized coping styles as productive and non-productive. Significantly, they concluded both styles decreased after brain injury. I’d posit that this decrease reflects reduced cognition from brain injury, which combined leads to a loss of self-worth.

Cardile et al wrote, “Dealing with ABI pathologies is often viewed as a stressful situation that presents many challenges. As a result, individuals may struggle to maintain control over their lives. Coping resources play a crucial role in preserving feelings of self-worth and managing the demands of the disease.”

As I relied on food as my central coping strategy, my self-worth nosedived. As the researchers noted, brain injury leads to a continual struggle to regain control over one’s life. One’s brain no longer works or responds to one’s intentions, while people react in unpredictable ways, blaming and abandoning. One cannot control others’ reactions nor what insurance (public and private) will cover; one can only fight for support and healthcare; but then brain injury fatigue, loss of stamina, and loss of multiple functions work against persisting. Eating is about the only thing one has control over; yet as a coping strategy it is, in effect, in control of you, not you of it.

In 2019, The Lancet published a call to change neurorehabilitation: “Acquired brain injury leaves survivors with a considerable burden of physical, cognitive, and psychosocial sequelae, and can also increase the risk of late neurodegenerative disease.”

This burden reduces coping capacity when most needed.

No matter where we live on the planet, people with brain injury need adaptive, productive coping capacities so that we can endure and heal from this devastating injury. Recognizing stress levels and assessing and teaching post-injury coping strategies isn’t enough; neurorehabilitation also needs to assess pre-injury coping styles and use effective treatments to rebuild former productive styles, support the use of active styles that include healthy distractions until they become automatic over the years, and reinforce taught productive styles. Since people with untreated brain injury struggle to retain habits and lessons, community care must continue to support existing styles and to innovate styles that adapt to changing brains, changing circumstances, and a changing world.

article continues after advertisement

In order to recover from brain injury, coping strategies help weather daily challenges and emotional upheavals or lack of affect, so that one can hunt down, endure, and benefit from objective diagnoses and effective treatments and reclaim one’s potential.

item.title: Gen Z Burnout Is a Workplace Story Not a Character Flaw
item.description:
Burnout

Gen Z Burnout Is a Workplace Story Not a Character Flaw

Gen Z questions burnout as the price of success.

Posted August 18, 2026

Key points
  • Gen Z’s workplace attitude reflects the world they entered, not a lack of motivation or work ethic.
  • Gen Z values meaningful work, psychological safety, flexibility, and work-life balance.
  • Burnout grows when workplace demands exceed the support, resources, and flexibility offered to employees.
  • Healthier workplaces address burnout at its source instead of relying on employees to cope.

Co-authored by Kennedy Hack-Juman & Amy Vigliotti, Ph.D.

As the newest members of the workforce, Generation Z has become the generation most often associated with burnout. Some interpret this as evidence that Gen Z "can't handle work," but there may be another explanation. What happens when an entire generation comes of age during economic uncertainty, social instability, a full-blown pandemic, and an unprecedented transfer to the remote world? Gen Z’s burnout may tell us less about their character than about the environment they have inherited.

Every generation is shaped by significant historical events, and Gen Z is no exception. The COVID-19 pandemic transformed adolescence, early adulthood, and work expectations. In particular, Gen Z learned to collaborate through breakout rooms, interview over Google Meet, and begin careers online. Beyond the pandemic, they also came of age in a time of rising political polarization and climate change, reinforcing a broader environment in which uncertainty became the norm.

These experiences had an impact. According to Karl Mannheim's theory of generations, the events people experience while coming of age shape the values and expectations they carry into adulthood (Harari et al., 2023). For Gen Z, these events also coincided with disruptions to education, work, and social development. Harari and colleagues (2023) found that although Gen Z reported lower resilience during the pandemic, they also showed more openness to change, one of the strongest predictors of resilience. That same openness to change was reflected in their preference for hybrid learning and workplace training, suggesting that the environments in which they came of age continue to shape their expectations from work today.

Source: Emily Underworld / Unsplash

Gen Z is also more transparent about mental health and burnout, which changes how burnout is recognized. As the stigma surrounding mental health has decreased, people are more likely to label their exhaustion, stress, and anxiety as “burnout” rather than weakness. Compared to Gen X and millennials, Gen Z reports lower levels of mental health stigma, reflecting more accepting attitudes towards mental health challenges (Camarillo et al., 2025).

These shifting attitudes also shape how Gen Z approaches the workplace. In a review examining multiple generations and their differences in burnout, Gen Z placed greater value on psychological safety, work-life balance, structured mentorship, and transparent communication. Overall, they are less willing to accept chronic overwork as the price of professional success (Molwitz et al., 2026). Older workplace cultures have often treated long hours and personal sacrifice as signs of professional dedication, which can make Gen Z’s requests for flexibility appear unmotivated or even entitled.

However, the research suggests that Gen Z is not less motivated. Instead, they are challenging the assumption that chronic overwork is a measure of dedication. Using the Job Demands-Resources model, Chen and colleagues (2023) argue that burnout is more likely to develop when chronic job demands outweigh available resources. In other words, burnout is not simply an inability to tolerate stress; it can emerge when the demands of a workplace constantly exceed the support, flexibility, and resources available to employees. The researchers found that Gen Z employees’ burnout is caused by excessive workload, long work hours, and limited organizational support. One extreme example is “996” work culture, in which employees work from 9 a.m. to 9 p.m., six days a week. This kind of chronic overwork increases burnout and contributes to greater psychological distress.

Individual coping strategies like mindfulness, healthy boundaries, and stress management matter, but they cannot replace healthy workplaces that combat burnout. Organizations can reduce burnout by addressing its causes rather than expecting employees to cope with it. Flexibility, healthy leadership, transparent communication, psychological safety, and manageable workloads benefit not only Gen Z, but employees across every generation.

Research can describe generational patterns but not always capture how those patterns feel to the people living them. We asked several Gen Z college students to describe their experiences. (We have used initials to protect their identities.)

What is one misconception people have about Gen Z at work?

JBW: People say that Gen Z doesn't want to work. I don't think that's true. We want careers that are meaningful and sustainable, and we're less willing to accept burnout as a normal part of success. That might come across as a lack of commitment, but really it’s just a different definition of what a healthy career looks like.

What do you wish older generations understood about burnout?

AP: I wish older generations took into account that we’re entering the workforce after 12 to 16+ years of being students. School teaches you to absorb information, and work expects you to produce results.

What do you do to prevent burnout at work?

JZ: I prioritize my workload by getting more important and time-consuming tasks out of the way first. I stick to a calendar to ensure not to overbook myself. I set my boundaries between work and personal life by communicating clearly about my availability and making sure to recharge outside of work so I can stay productive and focused.

JBW: I work for a start-up that has blurred work-life boundaries. Working hours feel like “suggestions,” and the expectation is for employees to dedicate as much time as possible to the mission. To combat this, I try to take advantage of the more flexible nature of a start-up. I frequently go on quick walks outside and make a point to get up from my desk. I also like to prioritize being social, even on weekdays.

Source: Vitaly Gariev / Unsplash

These students' experiences support what we see in the research on burnout. If we listen closely, Gen Z isn't asking for less work. Gen Z wants sustainable careers. Experiencing unusual levels of disruption and uncertainty has shaped their expectations and their understanding of what is needed for long-term stability in the workplace. Rather than dismissing this perspective, employers have an opportunity to adapt and learn from it. If Gen Z is questioning workplace norms, maybe the question isn’t whether this generation needs to change. It is whether the workplace is finally ready to evolve alongside it.
